articles.title: 35 Hilarious Reading Memes for Bookworms Who Have No Shelf-Control
articles.content:
在这个世界上，人分为两类：读书人和叹息“要是有时间读书就好了”的人。如果你属于前者，这些与阅读相关的梗图就是为你准备的。你们这些书虫无论在何处都能抱着一本好书——沙发上、海滩上、飞机上、机动车辆管理所的候车室里，甚至在婚礼宴席上（传闻如此）。

我对完美夏日有着自己的定义：躺在沙滩上，手捧着一本夏日畅销书，最好是埃琳·希尔德布兰德（Elin Hilderbrand）的作品。嘿，我必须得知道南塔基特岛上那些疯孩子们又在搞什么鬼……直到我的Kobo电子阅读器没电了。那不是我去海里游泳的时刻——而是我切换到iPhone手机上，发起梗图狂欢的时候。其他人都在水里涮脚，而我却独自坐在遮阳伞下，为自己最喜欢的娱乐方式捧腹大笑。

要知道，做一个读者不仅仅是一种爱好，而是一种完整的生活方式。这是你本来就堆满了的待读书单上每天新增的几本；这是你在Libby（图书借阅应用）上申请的书籍，像你自己策划的惊喜派对一样一起到来；这是为虚构角色的胜利欢呼时，却忘记给妈妈过生日送祝福。而没有什么能比书梗更好地捕捉这种既美妙又疯狂的生活方式——那些让人一看就“原来如此”的小方框。

所以，把你手头正在读的书放下（就一分钟，这章节会等你的，我保证），然后来浏览这些关于阅读、书籍和那些以完全正常的程度爱书的人的梗图吧。看完后，把它们发给你的书友，因为只有他们才能理解你的心情！

《读者文摘》的“阅读热讯”邮件订阅中，有更多关于幽默、书籍、清洁、旅行、科技和有趣事实的内容，每周为你送上精彩。

未读的书不是积压货，而是收藏品。别用那种眼神看着我，帮我拆开这盒从Bookshop新买来的书吧！
睡眠是暂时的，了解安娜·卡列尼娜的结局才是永恒的。
有些罪行是小事，有些则是……送这张读书梗图给那些背叛你的家伙吧。
新的照明设备，还是那个我。
图书馆的等待名单是我唯一能稳赢的彩票。
呃，去了再说买洗发水吧。但那本书能不能有货就不一定了！
那47本未读书不是在生气，只是失望罢了。
承认自己有问题是第一步，买下续集才是第二步。
“电量不足”是有史以来最悲伤的转折情节。
那是最好的系列书，现在却结束了。结束了！我该怎么办？
我知道自己是什么样子，好吗？而且，我的朋友是虚构的，不是幻想的。
我已经唠叨了20分钟，还会继续唠叨20分钟。
我尊重所有的生活方式……除了或许像你的。
我一直在看着你。记住这一点！
我在浏览，我说的。不是在购物，我说的。
这很真实。我就想说这句话。太真实了。
书签是免费的，收据是免费的。任何一张纸都免费。哎呀，我在大声嚷嚷吗？
大海明天还会在那里。南塔基特岛的三角恋需要我现在就去解决。
新书是赌博，而这本书从未让我失望过，是的，我每次读到第14章都会哭。
等等，等等，等等——让我舒服一点！
慢慢来！别着急！！！
是的。下一个问题。
叫一个读者选出最喜欢的书，就像让父母选出最喜欢的孩子，但更难，因为有400个孩子。
我连锤子都拿不稳，但女孩总要做自己该做的事。
对不起——你说什么？！！！
书是最好的面膜。
这趟旅程会很漫长，很迷茫，但绝对值得来回翻阅363次。
不是你的问题——是我的问题。
字是相同的，但书却不一样！
阳光是给那些有计划的人的。
我们都读完书了吗？没有。我们都喝光了几瓶夏多奈酒吗？是的。
你真要杀了我，小鬼！
没有什么能比自设的毫无后果的截止日期更能激发读者的活力了。我知道你在骨子里都能感受到这个读书梗——别否认了。
来吧，你很清楚你喜欢它。
《读者文摘》已经讲了超过100年的笑话，在过去的20年里，由高级特邀编辑安迪·西蒙斯（Andy Simmons）编辑和审核，他曾是《国家灯笼报》的幽默编辑，也是《现在这才叫搞笑》的作者。我们曾因幽默获得过ASME奖，包括喜剧短句、恶作剧、双关语、漫画、独句笑话、敲门游戏、谜语、梗图、推文和令人捧腹大笑的杂志专栏故事，比如“这个美好的国家中的生活”、“一天的工作”、“笑声是最好的药”以及“偶像幽默”，以及在线收集的短笑话、爸爸笑话和糟糕的笑话，以至于它们其实很精彩。你可以在我们2022年的文集《读者文摘：笑声是最好的药》中找到一个世纪的幽默。这篇关于读书梗的文章，劳拉·贝克（Laura Beck）利用了她作为电视节目和杂志专业幽默作家超过15年的经验。阅读更多关于我们团队、我们的贡献者和我们的编辑政策的内容。
原文由《读者文摘》首发：《35个搞笑的读书梗图，为那些没有“书架自控能力”的书虫准备》。
articles.summary:
There are two kinds of people in this world: people who read and people who say, “I wish I had time to read.” If you’re in the first camp, these reading memes are for you. You are the bookworms who will curl up with a good book literally anywhere—the couch, the beach, the plane, the DMV waiting room, a wedding reception (allegedly).

My perfect summer day? Parked in the sand with a beach read, preferably Elin Hilderbrand. Hey, I’ve gotta know what those crazy kids in Nantucket are up to … until my Kobo dies. That’s when I go into the water. Just kidding—that’s when I switch to my iPhone and bust out the memes. Everyone else is dipping their toes in the water, and I’m cackling alone under my umbrella about my favorite pastime.

Because here’s the thing about being a reader: It isn’t a hobby; it’s a full-on lifestyle. It’s the already-too-big TBR pile you add to daily. It’s the Libby holds that all arrive at once like a surprise party you scheduled yourself. It’s celebrating fictional characters’ wins while forgetting to call your mom on her actual birthday. And nothing captures this beautiful bonkers lifestyle quite like book memes—those perfect little squares of “yep, that’s me.”

So put down your current read (just for a minute—the chapter will wait, I promise), and scroll through these memes about reading, books and the people who love them a completely normal amount. When you’re done, send them to your book club, the only humans who could possibly understand what it’s like to be you!

Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more humor, books, cleaning, travel, tech and fun facts all week long.

The unread books aren’t a backlog. They’re a collection. Oh, stop looking at me like that and help me open this new box from Bookshop, will you?

Admitting you have a problem is the first step. Buying the sequel to that problem is the second.

“Battery low” is the saddest plot twist ever written.

Beach day, by the book

The “favorite book” question from hell

Asking a reader to pick a favorite book is like asking a parent to pick a favorite child, except way harder because there are 400 children.

If you build it, they will come

I can barely hold a hammer, but a girl’s gotta do what a girl’s gotta do.

The plot-twist physical reaction

articles.title: Here’s What “Old Book Smell” Actually Is—And Why We Love It So Much
articles.content:
我小时候是个非常紧绷的孩子，基本上需要一只小毛绒玩具、固定的日常规律和睡前全面的复盘才能正常运作。而图书馆是为数不多能让我的神经系统完全放松下来的地方之一。那种让我当时感到放松、至今仍能安抚我的主要因素之一，就是图书馆——尤其是旧书——的气味。

你知道我所指的那种气味：当你翻开一本比你年龄还大的平装本时，那种辛辣、暗淡、陈旧的香气瞬间涌入鼻腔。这种对特定书香的偏爱甚至有一个专门的名称：书腥症（bibliosmia）。这个词在2014年由英语教授奥利弗·蒂尔（Oliver Tearle）创造，他将希腊语中"书"和"气味"的词根结合起来，用以描述人们从旧书页中嗅到特殊香气时所感到的独特快感。如果你曾经在跳蚤市场上发现自己将鼻子深深埋进一本二手平装本中，那么恭喜你——你就是一名书腥症患者，并且你身处一群志趣相投的爱书人之中。实际上，有太多人爱好这种气味，以至于有一家香水品牌推出了"旧书"和"平装本"香气的香水，这样你就可以全天候拥有图书馆内部的气味了（不做评判，我会穿戴它的）。

但是，关于这种"旧书气味"（以及"新书气味"）为何让我们如此着迷呢？为此，我采访了拉布·纳瓦兹·汗医生（Rab Nawaz Khan, MD），他是一位既是神经科专科医生又是狂热的书迷。没错，这是一种真实的现象，而答案令人愉悦地充满智趣。

阅读下文，了解关于这种气味中具体发生了什么，以及是否真的可以安全地将脸埋进100年前的小说中（剧透：大多数情况下可以，大多数情况下可以）。

如果你在一群读者中询问"旧书气味"的描述，就像参加葡萄酒品鉴会一样。人们会使用类似葡萄酒专家的语言——音调、层次、顶部和基础——而事实证明，这种表达方式非常准确。而且每个人的回答都独一无二。

"我会将其描述为温暖、木质、略带甜味、灰尘飞扬，有时还带有一丝香草味，伴随着潜在的霉味，" 汗医生说。"具体气味会因纸张、墨水、装订、储存条件和年龄的不同而有所变化。"

雪耶娜·威廉姆斯（Cheyenne Williams）是一位书籍制作人，也是黑暗幻想订阅盒Everlore Hollow的联合创始人。她对书籍的气味如此着迷，以至于为她的公司每月发出的包裹都创造独特的香气，因此她以更细致的方式思考这个问题。对她来说，这种气味具有层次感。"一开始，有一种干燥、纸质的甜味，让我想起稻草，" 她说。"然后是更温暖的部分：香草和杏仁。在所有这些之下，是一种柔和、灰尘飞扬的麝香，带有一丝泥土气息。"

这种基调——那种麝香般、泥土般的气味——正是人们真正追求的，当他们说想要某种东西闻起来"旧"的时候。这也是最难把握的音调。"太多的话，它会散发出霉味或男士古龙水的气味，" 威廉姆斯说。"但是当它被甜味调和时，它会变得柔软和舒适。"

另一方面，新书闻起来几乎与这种气味毫不相同。翻开一本崭新的精装本——也许是今年夏天最好的沙滩读物之一——你所闻到的更接近于新油漆的味道，而不是图书馆：清新、带有一些化学气味，偶尔还会有点锋利。这并不是缺陷。它只是使用了完全不同的一组成分，我们稍后会详细讨论。

无论"旧书气味"由什么分子组成，都无法完全解释为什么如此多的人对此如此着迷。有很多原因让人们喜欢这种独特的气味。让我们从大脑开始，而不仅仅是鼻子。

"旧书的气味可能会瞬间唤起图书馆、学校、家庭书房或安静阅读的回忆，因此这份快乐部分来自于怀旧和情感联系，" 汗医生说。

威廉姆斯同意这一点："记忆是其中的重要部分。一股气味可以让你在意识到之前就回到某个地方。" 对于很多人来说，旧书与"童年图书馆、祖父母的书架，或者仅仅是一种安静和安全的感觉"有着密切联系。

这不仅仅是一种氛围。怀旧是一种强大的良药。

喜爱旧书的气味不仅是一种性格特征，更是一种化学反应。"气味与大脑中涉及情感和自传式记忆的神经网络有着异常紧密的联系，" 汗医生说，他研究过气味在大脑中的作用。他解释道，与其他感官不同，气味有一条相对直接的通路通向大脑中处理情感的部分，而视觉和听觉则需要经过更多的处理。这种捷径是为什么气味能在你意识到自己闻到什么之前就触发情感的部分原因。

这不仅仅是怀旧。威廉姆斯指出，旧书气味中的特定音调——香草、杏仁、木质——是我们大脑早已准备好喜欢的。"香草和杏仁让我们联想到烘焙和温暖，" 她说，"而纸张、木质和柔软的麝香使这种香气特别属于书籍。"

有一个理由让食物的气味与其他气味不同。一项发表在《人类神经科学前沿》上的脑成像研究发现，与食物相关的气味——比如人们在旧书中嗅到的香草和杏仁音调——以一种非食物气味通常不具备的方式激活了大脑中的多巴胺驱动的奖励回路。因此，你着迷的部分确实是纯粹的怀旧，而另一部分则是你的大脑在安静地奖励你，因为你闻到了某些东西，老实说，这让你想起了温暖的巧克力饼干。

"旧书气味"基本上已经操纵了游戏规则，使自己占据优势地位。

好的，现在是你一直期待的时刻。从化学角度来看，具体是什么使得一本40年前的平装本闻起来像烘焙店和篝火的结合体？

这里有一个有趣的事实，你需要知道："随着纸张老化，纤维素（木纤维）和木质素会缓慢分解并释放挥发性有机化合物（VOCs），" 汗医生说。这就是你闻到的气味。

松树、云杉和桉树是制造纸张时最常用的木材，而木质素是一种天然化合物，存在于大多数纸张的木浆中。威廉姆斯解释了为什么这一点如此重要："木质素存在于木浆纸中，随着老化会产生甜味。这正是部分香草气味的来源。这也是为什么用便宜木浆纸制作的书籍比用破布纸制作的书籍更有气味的原因。"

破布纸正如其名：用棉或亚麻纤维制作的纸张——实际上是旧布料——而不是用树木。它曾是19世纪之前欧洲和北美的标准纸张，至今仍被用于精美艺术印刷和档案文件。由于它是由棉或亚麻制成，而不是由木材制成，破布纸一开始几乎没有或没有木质素，这就是为什么无论它在架子上放置多少年，几乎不会发黄或产生那种经典的霉味。

纸质书籍随着木质素的分解，逐渐发展出这种独特的气味，而主要有四种天然分子提供了这些气味：

此外，不仅仅是纸张内部。"墨水、胶水、皮革和布面装订随着时间推移会以不同的方式老化并贡献自己的气味，" 威廉姆斯说。"然后还有书籍从环境中吸收的一切：灰尘、湿度，有时还有霉菌或霉味。"（稍后会更详细地讨论这个霉菌问题。）

新书尚未经历这种缓慢的分解过程。而不是几十年的化学分解，你闻到的是制造过程本身的新鲜副产品：来自墨水的溶剂，用于处理和漂白纸张的化学物质，以及用于装订的胶水，据科学历史研究所称。这是文学版的"新车气味"——愉快、略带锋利，并在几年内随着书籍进入其更缓慢、更霉味的退休阶段而消失。

所有用于书籍制造的墨水溶剂、纸张处理剂、胶水和其他物质的化合物都属于一个大类别：挥发性有机化合物，或VOCs。VOCs是可以在室温下轻易蒸发到空气中的碳基化合物。新书通常会释放最高浓度的这些化合物，仅仅因为它们刚刚印刷完成。但是，正如这两位专家所指出的，老化书籍也会产生自己的VOCs，只是通过几十年的缓慢分解而不是新的制造过程。

公平的问题，尤其是因为化学物质和霉菌在同一段落中出现。我们中的大多数人只知道VOCs是坏家伙——它们与新油漆、新地毯、新家具和那种新车气味背后的同一家族化学物质有关，美国环境保护署指出，这些气味在足够高的浓度下可能导致头痛、头晕、眼、鼻或喉咙刺激。但事实证明，只有部分VOCs有害，而这些通常不是书籍中发现的那种。

好消息是："普通纸张老化时释放的气味，来自一本干燥、清洁的书，在正常处理时不太可能造成伤害，" 汗医生说。书籍通常释放的VOCs浓度不足以对大多数人构成真正的健康风险。

环境刺激物则是另一回事。"灰尘和霉菌不同，因为颗粒和孢子可能刺激鼻子、眼睛、喉咙和肺部，" 汗医生说。"患有哮喘、霉菌过敏、慢性肺病或免疫力较弱的人应该避免刻意嗅闻明显发霉或严重霉味的书籍，并且不应在没有适当保护的情况下清理受污染的收藏。"

因此，你的日常二手平装本几乎可以随心所欲地嗅闻，就像你刚刚购买的新书一样。真正需要警惕的是那些潮湿、发霉的物品。

你可以通过书本本身来区分美妙的霉味和真正的问题。汗医生建议注意"强烈的潮湿、地下室般的气味、可见的绒毛状或粉末状生长、湿润或变形的页面、污渍，或页面粘连"。

他还补充说，你也应该注意身体发出的信号，因此要注意"在处理书籍时出现咳嗽、呼吸困难、眼睛瘙痒和鼻塞"。如果书籍表现出这些霉菌的迹象，汗医生建议将其与你的收藏隔离，或者彻底处理它，或者由保护专家评估，而不是继续处理或擦拭它。

威廉姆斯的说法更简洁："我非常不科学的经验法则是：温暖、甜蜜和干燥是美丽的化学老化。锋利、怪异和潮湿意味着要小心处理。"

我选择将其视为可以继续将鼻子贴在每个经过的书架上的许可，只要没有绒毛状物。我们在图书馆见！
articles.summary:
I was a very tightly wound child. I basically needed a stuffie, a set routine and a full daily debrief before bed just to function. And the library was one of the only places that could get my nervous system to stand all the way down. A huge part of what was so relaxing to me then, and still soothes me now, is the smell of the library—especially the smell of old books.

You know the one: that spicy, dusky, stale perfume that rises up the second you crack open a paperback older than you. There’s even a word for this specific breed of book love: bibliosmia. It was coined in 2014 by Oliver Tearle, an English professor who mashed together the Greek words for book and smell to describe the particular joy of sniffing old pages. If you’ve ever caught yourself burying your nose in a used paperback at a garage sale, congratulations—you’re a bibliosmiac, and you’re in excellent company. In fact, so many of us love this smell that one perfumery sells both an “Old Book” and a “Paperback” scent, so you can smell like the inside of a library 24/7 if that’s the life you want to live. (No judgment. I’d wear it.)

But what is about “old book smell“—and “new book smell,” for that matter—that makes us lose our minds? I spoke with Rab Nawaz Khan, MD, who is both a board-certified neurologist and devoted book lover, to find out. Yes, it’s a real phenomenon, and the answer is delightfully nerdy.

Read on to find out exactly what’s going on inside that smell, as well as whether it’s actually OK to keep shoving your face into 100-year-old novels. (Spoiler: Mostly yes. Mostly.)

Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more books, fun facts, humor, cleaning, travel and tech all week long.

What do books smell like, exactly?

If you ask a room full of readers to describe “old book smell,” it’s like going to a wine tasting. People reach for the same kind of language sommeliers use—notes, layers, top and base—and it turns out that’s a pretty accurate way to talk about it. And everyone’s answer is unique.

“I would describe it as warm, woody, slightly sweet, dusty and sometimes faintly vanilla-like, with an underlying mustiness,” Dr. Khan says. “The exact smell varies with the paper, ink, binding, storage conditions and age.”

Cheyenne Williams, a bookmaker and the co-founder of the dark-fantasy subscription box Everlore Hollow, is so into how her books smell that she creates a unique scent for every box her company sends out, so she thinks about this in even more detail. To her, it comes in layers. “At first, there’s a dry, papery sweetness that reminds me a little of hay,” she says. “Then you get the warmer part: vanilla and almond. Underneath all of that is a soft, dusty musk with a faint earthiness to it.”

That base note—the musky, earthy one—is what everyone’s really chasing when they say they want something to smell “old.” It’s also the hardest note to get right. “Too much and it smells like mildew or men’s cologne,” Williams says. “When it’s balanced by the sweeter notes, though, it becomes soft and comforting.”

New books, meanwhile, smell almost nothing like this. Crack open a brand-new hardcover—maybe one of this summer’s best beach reads—and what you’re smelling is closer to fresh paint than a library: crisp, a little chemical, occasionally downright sharp. That’s not a flaw. It’s just an entirely different set of ingredients, which we’ll get into shortly.

Why do we love “old book smell” so much?

Whatever “old book smell” is made of, molecule for molecule, doesn’t fully explain why so many of us go a little weak in the knees over it. There are a number of reasons why people love that distinctive smell. Let’s start by looking at what’s happening in your brain, not just your nose.

It’s mostly about memory

“An old-book scent may instantly bring back libraries, school, family homes or quiet reading, so part of the pleasure comes from nostalgia and emotional association,” Dr. Khan says.

Williams agrees: “Memory is a huge part of it. A scent can bring you back to a place before you’ve even consciously identified it.” For a lot of people, she adds, old books are tied to “childhood libraries, a grandparent’s bookshelf or simply the feeling of being somewhere quiet and safe.”

And it isn’t just a vibe. Nostalgia is powerful medicine.

There’s real brain chemistry behind it too

Loving the smell of an old book isn’t just a personality quirk—it’s chemistry. “Smell has unusually strong links with brain networks involved in emotion and autobiographical memory,” says Dr. Khan, who has studied how smell works in the brain. He explains that smell is unique among the senses in that it has a fairly direct line to the parts of the brain that handle emotion, while sight and sound get routed through more processing first. That shortcut is part of why a scent can trigger a feeling before you’ve even consciously identified what you’re smelling.

It’s not only nostalgia, though. Williams points out that the specific notes in old book smell—vanilla, almond, wood—are ones our brains are already primed to enjoy. “Vanilla and almond remind us of baking and warmth,” she says, “while the paper, wood and soft musk make the fragrance feel specific to books.”

There’s a reason food smells hit differently than other odors. A brain-imaging study published in Frontiers in Human Neuroscience found that food-associated scents—like the vanilla and almond notes people pick up in old books—activate the brain’s dopamine-driven reward circuitry in a way that nonfood smells generally don’t. So part of what you’re falling for really is pure nostalgia, and part of it is your brain quietly rewarding you for smelling something that, honestly, reminds you of warm chocolate chip cookies.

“Old book smell” has basically rigged the game in its own favor.

So what actually makes books smell the way they do?

All right, it’s the moment you’ve been waiting for. What is actually happening, chemically, to make a 40-year-old paperback smell like a bakery had a baby with a campfire?

Old books

Here’s the first fun fact you need to know: “As paper ages, cellulose (wood fiber) and lignin slowly break down and release volatile organic compounds, or VOCs,” Dr. Khan says. That’s what you’re smelling.

Pine, spruce and eucalyptus are the most common woods used in making paper, and lignin is a natural compound found in the wood pulp that most paper is made from. Williams explains why this matters so much: “Lignin, which is found in wood-pulp paper, produces a sweet smell as it ages. That’s where some of the vanilla-like character comes from. It’s also why books made from cheap wood-pulp paper can have a stronger smell than books made from rag paper.”

Rag paper is exactly what it sounds like: paper made from cotton or linen fibers—literally old cloth rags—instead of from trees. It was the standard paper used in Europe and North America before the 19th century, and it’s still prized today for fine-art prints and archival documents. Because it comes from cotton or linen rather than wood, rag paper starts out with little to no lignin in it, which is why it barely yellows or develops that classic musty smell, no matter how many decades it sits on a shelf.

Paper books develop that signature smell as lignin breaks down, and there are four main naturally occurring molecules that provide the smells:

  • Vanillin, the same compound that gives real vanilla beans their scent and why books kind of smell like cookies.
  • Benzaldehyde, which provides the faint almond note, adding to the cookie smell.
  • Furfural, which is described as smelling like toasted bread. It also has a practical purpose: A University College London study on the chemistry of old books used furfural as a marker to measure how degraded a piece of paper actually is, essentially “diagnosing” a book’s condition by its smell alone.
  • Guaiacol, which adds a faint smoky or spicy note. It’s the same compound largely responsible for the smoky notes in whiskey, roasted coffee and campfire smoke, which is exactly why a well-aged book can carry a faint whiff of fireplace along with its vanilla.

And it’s not only what’s inside the paper. “Ink, glue, leather and cloth bindings all age differently and contribute their own scents,” Williams says. “Then there’s everything a book picks up from its environment over the years: dust, humidity and, sometimes, mold or mildew.” (More on that mold business shortly.)

New books

New books don’t have that slow decomposition yet. Instead of decades of chemical breakdown, what you’re smelling is the fresh by-product of the manufacturing process itself: solvents from the ink, chemicals used to treat and bleach the paper, and the adhesives holding the binding together, according to the Science History Institute. It’s the literary version of new-car smell—pleasant, a little sharp and gone within a few years as the book settles into its slower, mustier retirement.

All of the ink solvents, paper treatments, glue and other things used in book manufacturing have compounds that fall under one big umbrella: volatile organic compounds, or VOCs. VOCs are carbon-based chemicals that evaporate easily into the air at room temperature. New books tend to release the highest concentration of them, simply because they’re fresh off the press, but as both experts note, aging books produce their own VOCs too, just through decades of slow decay instead of fresh manufacturing.

Hold on—are those things OK to breathe in?

Fair question, especially since chemical compounds and mold showed up in the same paragraph above. Most of us only know VOCs as the bad guys—they’re the same family of chemicals behind the noxious off-gassing smell of fresh paint, new carpet, new furniture and that brand-new-car scent, which the Environmental Protection Agency notes can cause headaches, dizziness, and eye, nose or throat irritation at high enough concentrations. But it turns out that only some VOCs are harmful, and those generally aren’t the ones found in books.

The good news: “Normal aged-paper odor from a clean, dry book is unlikely to be harmful during ordinary handling,” Dr. Khan says. The VOCs that an average book gives off simply aren’t concentrated enough to pose a real health risk to most people.

Environmental irritants are a different story, though. “Dust and mold are different because particles and spores can irritate the nose, eyes, throat and lungs,” Dr. Khan says. “People with asthma, mold allergy, chronic lung disease or weakened immunity should avoid deliberately sniffing visibly moldy or heavily musty books and should not clean contaminated collections without appropriate protection.”

So your everyday secondhand paperback is almost certainly fine to sniff to your heart’s content, as is that new book you just bought. It’s the genuinely damp, moldy stuff you want to watch out for.

How will you know if your “old book smell” has crossed a line?

You can tell the difference between wonderfully musty and actual problem by the book itself. Dr. Khan recommends watching out for “a strong damp, basement-like odor, visible fuzzy or powdery growth, wet or warped pages, staining, or pages sticking together.”

You also should pay attention to what your body is telling you, he adds, so note any “coughing, wheezing, itchy eyes and congestion while handling the book.” If a book is showing those signs of mold, Dr. Khan suggests isolating it from the rest of your collection and either getting rid of it or having it assessed by a conservator, rather than continuing to handle or brush it off yourself.

Williams puts it more simply: “My very unscientific rule of thumb is: warm, sweet and dry is the beautiful chemistry of aging. Sharp, funky and wet means handle with care.”

I’m choosing to take that as permission to keep pressing my nose into every book-filled shelf I pass, so long as nothing’s fuzzy. See you at the library!

About the experts

  • Rab Nawaz Khan, MD, is a board-certified neurologist with more than a decade of clinical experience. His practice focuses on stroke care, neurology and neurorehabilitation, and he contributes health and brain-science content to MyMigraineTeam.
  • Cheyenne Williams is a bookmaker and the co-founder of Everlore Hollow, a serialized dark-fantasy mystery subscription box. She formulates and hand-pours the custom scents included in every box, aiming to capture scents that pull readers into the story.

Why trust us

At Reader’s Digest, we’re committed to producing high-quality content by writers with expertise and experience in their field in consultation with relevant, qualified experts. We rely on reputable primary sources, including government and professional organizations and academic institutions as well as our writers’ personal experiences where appropriate. For this piece on “old book smell,” Charlotte Hilton Andersen tapped her experience as a longtime journalist who frequently writes about common curiosities for Reader’s Digest. We verify all facts and data, back them with credible sourcing and revisit them over time to ensure they remain accurate and up to date. 8月，这个美食爱好者的天堂，似乎成了全国各地美食盛宴的非正式主题月。当你以为夏日烧烤已经让你吃到撑的时候，8月的美食节却带来了黄油大龙虾、烟熏烧烤和各种让你垂涎欲滴的美食。说真的，如果你有喜欢的美食，肯定会有一个地方的美食节在庆祝它。

8月是丰收的高峰季节，农田里水果蔬菜丰收，甜玉米、多汁的桃子、成熟的西红柿、浆果以及其他夏日盛宴的食材应有尽有。加上温暖的天气和户外节日季节，8月成为了一年中美食节最繁忙的一个月。唯一的遗憾是，除非你有无限的假期和钢铁般的胃（当然不可能），你不可能参加所有的美食节。因此，我们精选了最好的节日，并按照地区分类，方便大家规划行程。

以下是今年8月值得一看的美食节（建议穿着有点弹性的裤子，信我，你会需要的）。

**Smorgasburg（纽约）**
活动时间：4月2日-10月25日
作为纽约美食节中最受欢迎的之一，Smorgasburg不仅仅是一个美食市场，更是周末的传统活动，也是品尝纽约美食的最佳方式之一。这个户外美食节从春季一直持续到秋季，在多个城市角落出现，为你提供探索纽约不同街区的绝佳理由。2026年，你可以在周五的世界贸易中心分店、周六的威廉斯堡分店和周日的布鲁克林展望公园分店享受不同的美食体验，每个分店都有数十家轮换的摊位和独特的街区氛围。

在这里，你可以品尝到哥伦比亚的阿莱帕和烤肉、韩国烧烤碗、藏式饺子、油炸汤包、松露薯条等，以及手工冰淇淋三明治、韩国冰淇淋、其他夸张的甜品。

**缅因龙虾节（缅因州）**
活动时间：7月29日-8月2日
如果海鲜是你的最爱，这个免费的8月美食节应该列入你的夏日清单之首。（但要赶紧，因为它只持续到本月的第一个周末！）在缅因州美丽的海岸线上，缅因龙虾节用各种方式呈现新鲜龙虾——从经典的蒸龙虾、黄油龙虾堡到奶油龙虾千层面。除了美食，你还可以参加烹饪比赛、音乐会、游行、家庭友好活动，以及让你忍不住想多待一天的海滨风景。记得来的要饥肠辘辘，因为你可能会离开时后悔没多吃点龙虾。

**全美水牛城鸡翅节（水牛城）**
活动时间：8月29日-8月30日
或许没有比发明鸡翅的城市更好的地方来庆祝鸡翅节了。全美水牛城鸡翅节汇聚了数十家鸡翅摊位，提供从经典的水牛城风格鸡翅到你闻所未闻的创意风味鸡翅。配上现场音乐、冰镇饮料，还有机会参与解决水牛城最佳鸡翅的争议。除了美食，节日还包括美国鸡翅大赛、超辣鸡翅挑战赛和有趣的蓝酪挑战赛等吸引人气的传统活动。

**爱荷华甜玉米节（爱荷华州）**
活动时间：8月8日
如果你从未吃过爱荷华州的甜玉米，那你确实错过了人生。这个免费的一天活动完全致力于新鲜玉米，配上黄油，证明了一点黄油的魔力。加上当地的食品摊位、手工摊位、社区活动和经典的节日零食，你会发现这是一个既像家乡庆典又像美食节的完美日子。

活动实际上从前一天晚上开始，社区壳玉米的传统让志愿者们为第二天的免费派发准备了数千个玉米棒。节日当天，繁华的市中心游行、5公里跑、免费甜玉米（数量有限）、现场表演、儿童活动、汽车展和街头音乐会让这个节日充满了活力。

**印第安纳州州博览会（印第安纳州）**
活动时间：8月7日-8月23日
是的，这是一个州博览会，但美食爱好者知道这就是为什么你应该去。除了经典的炸食，你还可以品尝到猪排三明治、烤玉米、乳制品甜品、自制馅饼和接近50种全新的食品和饮料创意，以及许多经济实惠的美食选择。除了美食，你还可以观看音乐会、探索农业展览，并登上叙事性的州博览会列车，轻松游览博览会场地。

新的亮点包括“总是一个全垒打”，这是一个互动的棒球主题体验，庆祝印第安纳州与印第安纳波利斯印第安人队的丰富棒球历史，“倒带：VHS复兴”则带你回到录像带租赁店的时代，充满了稀有收藏品和复古氛围。家庭还可以在空调开放的大帐篷马戏团下乘凉，那里有杂技演员和小丑每日表演，让你在美食和娱乐之间充实一天。门票为18美元，但提前在线购买则为14美元。

**芝加哥哈拉尔美食节（伊利诺伊州）**
活动时间：8月8日-8月9日
这个8月的美食节，你最大的挑战就是决定先吃什么。在凯恩县博览会场地举行的芝加哥哈拉尔美食节，汇集了30多家哈拉尔美食摊位、当地餐厅和甜点制作者，庆祝全球各地的风味。凭借40美元的门票，你可以品尝到从正宗波斯烤肉、肖华玛和法拉法到南亚街头美食、乌兹别克特色菜、泰国美食、哈拉尔压碎汉堡、加载薯条和各种甜点。除了美食，你还可以期待现场表演、当地摊主的产品和适合全家人的欢乐氛围，使其成为中西部最受欢迎的夏季美食节之一。

**食客乐园美食节（田纳西州）**
活动时间：8月2日-8月30日
如果你梦想中的8月美食节是在一个周末内环游世界，那么纳什维尔的食客乐园美食节就是你的不二选择。这个流动的美食节驶入纳什维尔超级赛道附近的黎巴嫩，汇集了250多家美食摊位，提供从亚洲街头美食、烤肉串到夸张的甜点和当地美食。在美食之间，你可以浏览手工货品的艺术家摊位、享受现场DJ和游戏，沉浸在户外节日的欢乐氛围中。

更棒的是，如果你无法参加田纳西州的活动，食客乐园会巡回全国各地的城市——包括波特兰、孟菲斯、夏洛特和亚特兰大——所以值得关注它何时到达你附近的目的地。门票低于15美元，允许你随时入场。

**休斯顿美食节（德克萨斯州）**
活动时间：8月1日-9月7日
这可以算是吃遍休斯顿——美国最佳美食城市之一的绝佳理由。数百家餐厅提供固定价格的菜单，展示休斯敦令人惊叹的多样性，包括德州烧烤、墨西哥湾海鲜、正宗墨西哥美食和现代南方美食。更棒的是，每一餐都能为休斯敦食品银行筹集资金，因此你的晚餐也能做点好事。

**阿肯色州葡萄节（阿肯色州）**
活动时间：8月4日-8月8日
意大利传统遇见南方好客，这个阿肯色州的传统节日深受欢迎。期待自制意大利面晚餐、葡萄冰淇淋、炸馄饨、肉丸子、当地葡萄酒，当然还有丰富的葡萄。这是一个兼具美食节和社区庆典的活动，吸引着几代人的参与。这个节日的最受欢迎的传统之一是生动的葡萄踩踏活动，在这里，游客可以真正跳进去，感受活动的酿酒传统。

在本周晚些时候，由社区制作的意大利面晚餐成为焦点，提供几十年来成为节日标志的食谱。整个免费的活动周，游乐场的游戏和活动保持着高昂的气氛，而手工艺展销会则提供了当地摊主的手工制品。如果你想活动一下，你甚至可以在周六参加“为葡萄跑”5公里比赛，然后用一盘意大利面和一勺葡萄冰淇淋奖励自己。

**帕利赛德桃子节（科罗拉多州）**
活动时间：8月21日-8月22日
佐治亚州可能抢走了所有的桃子关注度，但科罗拉多州当地人知道帕利赛德桃子有多特别。这个愉快的节日庆祝该地区著名的水果，包括桃子派、桃子小饼、桃子莎莎、桃子冰淇淋和可以带回家的果园新鲜桃子。加上厨师表演、现场音乐和葡萄园景色，你就拥有了一个美味的周末。活动于周五开始，有现场表演、当地DJ和晚上的无人机表演点亮科罗拉多州西部的天空，而周六继续以更多的现场音乐和品尝桃子启发的美食为重点。

当然，没有人会错过经典的桃子大赛，或者带着一盒新鲜采摘的帕利赛德桃子离开，这样你就可以在节日结束后继续享受。你可以购买特定日期或周末套票，提前购买的周五成人门票价格低于25美元。

**俄勒冈州大蒜节（俄勒冈州）**
活动时间：8月7日-8月9日
蒜香薯条？蒜蓉面包？蒜蓉冰淇淋？如果它可以用大蒜制成，你在这里可能会找到它。俄勒冈州著名的大象蒜节庆祝该州巨大、温和的大蒜，有美食摊位、烹饪演示、当地产品和家庭友好娱乐。它非常奇妙，以一种最好的方式。冒险的食客可以尝试节日的著名蒜蓉冰淇淋，然后享受黄油蒜蓉面包、装满蒜蓉薯条和汉堡、鸡肉美食的丰盛篮子，以及其他用烤大象蒜制成的美味佳肴。

当地的美食卡车为经典节日食品增添了蒜蓉元素，而啤酒、葡萄酒和苹果酒园则提供了平衡这些大胆风味的完美方式。在你回家之前，别忘了从当地农民那里购买一些新鲜的大象蒜大蒜，这样你就可以在自己的厨房里重现一点节日的魔力。

**乔伊斯黑莓节（华盛顿州）**
活动时间：8月1日
小镇的魅力在这个华盛顿州奥林匹克半岛的小镇乔伊斯展现得淋漓尽致，这个备受喜爱的8月美食节已经将社区聚集在一起超过四十年。这个免费的一天庆祝活动以自制黑莓派闻名，这些派在早上开始销售，往往很快就售罄。来这里享用一顿丰盛的煎饼早餐或流行的鲑鱼烤肉，然后参加盛大的游行、当地的手工摊位和这个节日最奇特的传统之一：总是有趣的极端田螺比赛。

入场免费，食物、派和其他活动需要购买，这使得它成为一个轻松和实惠的夏日一日游。《读者文摘》已经发表了数百篇帮助读者安全、轻松和经济实惠地探索世界的旅行故事。我们经常涵盖的主题包括最佳旅行目的地（以及最佳旅行时间）、穿过机场安检的技巧和秘诀、空姐秘密、酒店房间技巧等。我们致力于生产高质量的内容，由具备领域专长和经验的作家撰写，并征求相关合格专家的意见。我们依赖于可靠的初级来源，包括政府和专业组织、学术机构以及适当情况下的作家的个人经验。我们核实所有事实和数据，以可信的出处为后盾，并定期重新审视以确保其准确性和及时性。了解更多关于我们团队、我们的贡献者和我们的编辑政策。
articles.summary:
I don’t know who decided August should become the unofficial month of eating your way across America, but I’m certainly not complaining. Just when you think you’ve had your fill of summer cookouts, August food festivals roll around with buttery lobster, smoky barbecue and just about every other crave-worthy bite you can think of. Seriously, if there’s a food you love, there’s probably a town somewhere throwing a party for it.

August is peak harvest season, so farms are overflowing with sweet corn, juicy peaches, ripe tomatoes, berries and just about every other summer favorite. Pair that with warm weather and outdoor festival season, and you’ve got one of the busiest months of the year for food festivals. The only downside? Unless you somehow have unlimited vacation days (and a stomach of steel), you can’t possibly hit them all. So we narrowed it down to the best of the best—and to make planning easier, we split them up by region.

Read on for some of the best August food festivals of the year. (I’d also recommend wearing pants with a little stretch. Trust me.)

Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more travel, food, fun facts, humor, cleaning, travel and tech all week long.

Northeast

Smorgasburg in New York City

When it runs: April 2–Oct. 25

One of my personal favorites, Smorgasburg isn’t just a food market—it’s a weekend tradition and one of the best ways to eat your way through New York City. Running from spring through fall, this open-air food festival pops up in multiple neighborhoods, giving you the perfect excuse to explore different corners of the city. In 2026, you can visit the World Trade Center location on Fridays, Williamsburg on Saturdays and Prospect Park in Brooklyn on Sundays, with each location featuring dozens of rotating vendors and its own unique neighborhood vibe.

You’ll find everything from Colombian arepas and grilled meats to Korean BBQ bowls, Tibetan momos, fried soup dumplings, truffle fries and more—not to mention artisanal ice cream sandwiches, Korean bingsoo and other over-the-top desserts.

LEARN MORE

Maine Lobster Festival in Rockland, Maine

When it runs: July 29–Aug. 2

If seafood is your love language, this free-to-enter August food festival belongs at the top of your summer bucket list. (But hurry, because it only runs through the first weekend of the month!) Held on Maine’s picturesque coast, the Maine Lobster Festival serves up fresh lobster every way imaginable—from classic steamed lobster and buttery lobster rolls to creamy lobster mac and cheese. Beyond the food, you’ll find cooking contests, live music, parades, family-friendly activities and waterfront views that make lingering all day feel like the obvious choice. Come hungry because you’ll probably leave wondering why you don’t eat lobster more often.

LEARN MORE

National Buffalo Wing Festival in Buffalo, New York

When it runs: Aug. 29–Aug. 30

There may be no better place to celebrate chicken wings than the city that invented them. The National Buffalo Wing Festival brings together dozens of wing vendors serving everything from classic Buffalo-style wings to creative flavors you probably never imagined. Pair your wings with live music, plenty of cold drinks and the chance to finally settle the age-old debate over who really makes Buffalo’s best wings. Beyond the food, the festival is packed with crowd-pleasing traditions, including the U.S. Chicken Wing Eating Championship, the fiery XXX Hot Wing Eating Challenge and the hilariously messy blue cheese bobbing contest that has become one of the event’s signature attractions.

LEARN MORE

Midwest

Sweet Corn Festival in Adel, Iowa

When it runs: Aug. 8

If you’ve never eaten Iowa sweet corn straight from the cob, prepare to be spoiled. This free one-day August celebration is all about freshly harvested corn served hot with butter, proving that it’s a-maize-ing what a little butter can do. Add local food vendors, craft booths, community events and classic fair treats, and you’ve got a day that’s equal parts hometown celebration and food festival.

The festivities actually kick off the night before with the community corn-shucking tradition, when volunteers prepare thousands of ears for the next day’s giveaway, setting the stage for the main event. Festival day brings a lively downtown parade, a 5K, free sweet corn while supplies last, live entertainment, kids activities, a car show and a street party with live music.

LEARN MORE

Indiana State Fair in Indianapolis, Indiana

When it runs: Aug. 7–Aug. 23

Yes, it’s a state fair—but food lovers know that’s exactly why you should go. Alongside deep-fried favorites, you’ll find pork tenderloin sandwiches, grilled corn, dairy treats, homemade pies and nearly 50 brand-new food and drink creations making their debut, plus plenty of budget-friendly bites on the fair’s popular $5 value menu. Beyond the food, you can catch live concerts, explore agricultural exhibits and hop aboard the narrated State Fair Train for a relaxing ride around the fairgrounds.

New attractions include Always a Hit, an interactive baseball-themed experience celebrating Indiana’s rich baseball history with the Indianapolis Indians, as well as Rewind: A VHS Revival, a nostalgic trip back to the video-store era complete with rare collectibles and retro vibes. Families can also cool off under the air-conditioned Big-Top Circus, where aerialists and clowns perform daily, making it easy to fill an entire day between great food and even better entertainment. General admission is $18, but buying early online is $14.

LEARN MORE

Chicagoland Halal Fest in St. Charles, Illinois

When it runs: Aug. 8–Aug. 9

This is one August food festival where your biggest challenge will be deciding what to eat first. Held at the Kane County Fairgrounds, the Chicagoland Halal Fest brings together more than 30 halal food vendors, local restaurants and dessert makers for a weekend celebrating flavors from around the world. With your $40 admission ticket, you can sample everything from authentic Persian kebabs, shawarma and falafel to South Asian street food, Uzbek specialties, Thai favorites, halal smash burgers, loaded fries and plenty of sweet treats. Beyond the incredible eats, expect live entertainment, products from local vendors and a lively, family-friendly atmosphere that makes this one of the Midwest’s most flavorful summer festivals.

LEARN MORE

South

The FoodieLand Food Festival in Nashville, Tennessee

When it runs: Aug. 2–Aug. 30

If your dream August food festival involves tasting your way around the world in a single weekend, the FoodieLand Food Festival in Nashville is the one for you. This traveling food festival rolls into the Nashville Superspeedway in nearby Lebanon with more than 250 food vendors serving everything from Asian street food and grilled skewers to over-the-top desserts and local favorites. Between bites, you can browse artisan vendors selling handmade goods, enjoy live DJs and games, and soak up the lively outdoor festival atmosphere.

Even better? If you can’t make the Tennessee stop, FoodieLand travels to cities across the country—including Portland, Memphis, Charlotte and Atlanta—so it’s worth checking the schedule to see when it’s coming to a destination near you. Admission is under $15, and tickets allow you to enter at any time.

LEARN MORE

Houston Restaurant Weeks in Houston, Texas

When it runs: Aug. 1–Sept. 7

Think of this as the ultimate excuse to eat your way across one of America’s best food cities. Hundreds of restaurants offer prix-fixe menus showcasing Houston’s incredible diversity. This includes Texas barbecue, Gulf Coast seafood, authentic Mexican and modern Southern cuisine. Better yet, every meal helps raise money for the Houston Food Bank, so your dinner does some good too.

LEARN MORE

Tontitown Grape Festival in Tontitown, Arkansas

When it runs: Aug. 4–Aug.8

Italian heritage meets Southern hospitality at this beloved Arkansas tradition. Expect homemade spaghetti dinners, grape ice cream, fried ravioli, meatballs, local wines and, of course, plenty of juicy grapes. It’s part food festival, part community celebration—and one that’s been drawing visitors for generations. One of the festival’s most beloved traditions is the lively grape stomp, where visitors can literally jump in feet-first and embrace the event’s winemaking roots.

Later in the week, the famous community-made spaghetti dinners take center stage, serving the recipes that have become a hallmark of the festival for decades. Throughout the free week, the carnival midway keeps the energy high with rides and games, while an arts-and-crafts fair offers handmade goods from local vendors. If you’re feeling active, you can even kick off Saturday with the Run for the Grapes 5K before rewarding yourself with a plate of spaghetti—and maybe a scoop of grape ice cream afterward.

LEARN MORE

West

Palisade Peach Festival in Palisade, Colorado

When it runs: Aug. 21–Aug. 22

Georgia may get all the peach attention, but Colorado locals know Palisade peaches are something special. This cheerful festival celebrates the region’s famous fruit with peach pies, peach cobbler, peach salsa, peach ice cream and orchard-fresh peaches you can take home. Throw in chef demonstrations, live music and vineyard views, and you’ve got one delicious weekend. The festivities kick off Friday with live performances, local DJs and an evening drone show lighting up the Western Colorado sky, while Saturday keeps the energy going with even more live music and plenty of opportunities to sample peach-inspired dishes from local chefs and food vendors.

Of course, no visit is complete without taking on the classic peach-eating contest—or leaving with a box of freshly picked Palisade peaches to enjoy long after the festival ends. You can purchase specific day or weekend packages, with pre-purchased Friday adult admission tickets going for less than $25.

LEARN MORE

Elephant Garlic Festival in North Plains, Oregon

When it runs: Aug. 7–Aug. 9

Garlic fries? Garlic bread? Garlic ice cream? If it can be infused with garlic, you’ll probably find it here. Oregon’s famous (and free!) Elephant Garlic Festival celebrates the state’s giant, mild garlic with food vendors, cooking demonstrations, local produce and family-friendly entertainment. It’s wonderfully weird—in the best possible way. Adventurous eaters can sample the festival’s famous garlic ice cream before diving into buttery garlic bread, overflowing baskets of garlic fries and burgers, chicken dishes and other savory favorites loaded with roasted elephant garlic.

Local food trucks put their own garlicky spin on fair classics, while the beer, wine and cider garden offers the perfect way to balance all those bold flavors. Before you head home, don’t forget to pick up a few fresh elephant garlic bulbs from area farmers so you can recreate a little festival magic in your own kitchen.

LEARN MORE

Joyce Daze Wild Blackberry Festival in Joyce,Washington

When it runs: Aug. 1

Small-town charm is on full display at the Joyce Daze Wild Blackberry Festival, a beloved August food festival that’s been bringing the community together for more than four decades. Held in the tiny town of Joyce on Washington’s Olympic Peninsula, the free one-day celebration is famous for its homemade blackberry pies, which go on sale in the morning and tend to disappear quickly. Come hungry for a hearty pancake breakfast or the popular salmon bake, then stick around for the grand parade, local craft vendors and one of the festival’s quirkiest traditions: the always-entertaining extreme slug races.

Admission is free, with food, pies and other activities available for purchase, making it an easy and affordable summer day trip.

articles.content:
近期因生菜引发的环孢子虫疫情和召回事件频发，是否让你对生吃沙拉产生了警惕？作为曾在食品安全实验室工作超过十年的专业人士，我完全理解这种忧虑。尽管工作中接触的高风险食品名单越来越长，但我始终没有放弃生吃水果蔬菜，因为正确的清洗方式往往是健康与疾病之间的关键分界线。

然而，问题在于我们在家庭厨房中往往会变得麻痹大意。虽然我们定期清洁厨房、及时擦拭溅落的食物，但一颗葡萄滚落水槽似乎不足为虑。但实际上，微生物并不关心"五秒规则"，也不会在意你的厨房看起来有多干净。即使你已经尽心尽力，仍可能因过时的安全建议或社交媒体上的时尚潮流而采取错误的做法。

为此，我采访了明尼苏达大学扩展服务的全州食品安全教育专家Amy Johnston，以及专门处理食源性疾病诉讼的律师Steve Wagner，为你剖析错误建议，提供基于科学的方法，以降低在准备新鲜水果蔬菜时患病的风险。

食品安全的第一步是确保工具干净：砧板、刀具、碗具和双手。FDA建议在清洗任何果蔬前后，用温水和肥皂洗手至少20秒。接下来，Johnston建议："务必花时间清洁和消毒水槽，包括水龙头、排水口和周围的台面。" 确保使用标有"食品安全"的消毒剂。

接下来要牢记的原则是只使用冷水流。Johnston解释说："温水或热水可能会导致某些果蔬受到冲击。"如果果蔬表面有任何污染物，这些物质可能会通过皮肤或果皮渗入你将要食用的果肉部分。Wagner补充说，肥皂的情况也是如此："绝对不要使用任何肥皂或洗衣粉，更不用说漂白剂了，因为果蔬会吸收残留物。"

对于能够承受的果蔬，使用专用刷子刷洗。Johnston说："这些刷毛可以深入缝隙，清除各种污染物和泥土。"

最后，需要明确的是，任何清洗程序都无法完全消除风险。这些安全措施已被证明能减少微生物的存在，但无法彻底消除。

Johnston指出："不幸的是，对于环孢子虫，唯一能消除它的方法是将果蔬加热至至少70℃（158℉）。" 这对于通常生吃的果蔬来说并不理想。Wagner补充说："人们以为洗一洗就能解决问题，但实际上更复杂。冲洗可以去除表面细菌，但寄生虫需要通过加热才能完全中和。"

Wagner表示，对于大肠杆菌或沙门氏菌，用流水冲洗并摩擦表面，同时保持4℃以下冷藏，通常足以应对非疫情期间。"但在当前疫情期间，要关注政府机构的公告，有些情况下可能需要暂时避免某种产品。"

目前这个建议尤其重要，特别是对于已经被列入疫情名单的袋装生菜等产品。通常，食品安全专家不建议重新清洗袋装果蔬，以避免交叉污染。但CDC现在建议清洗所有果蔬，无论何种情况。从本地农场购买整颗生菜，也能带来更大的安心感。

以下是清洗八大类水果蔬菜的正确方法：

长期以来，我习惯将水槽灌满水，浸泡菠菜、生菜和羽衣甘蓝以去除泥沙。但Johnston指出，这种做法可能反而会带来更多细菌。"如果果蔬上有污染物，浸泡可能会导致它们被吸收。" 因为这些嫩叶是多孔的（包括坚韧的羽衣甘蓝），在水中浸泡时会吸收污染物。

正确做法是去除外层的叶子，然后用冷流水冲洗其他部分。如果这些蔬菜来自你的菜园或农贸市场，你担心泥沙，可以进行"浸泡冲洗"。将叶类蔬菜放入大号滤网，然后反复浸入盛有冷水的大碗或干净的水槽中。倒干并用新鲜流水冲洗。

Wagner建议："坚果类蔬菜应在流水下用果蔬刷或洁净的双手刷洗，以去除任何病原体。" 但不要在购买后立即清洗，应等到食用或准备前。这有助于延长保存期限，减少提前腐烂的风险（适用于所有果蔬）。如果必须提前清洗，比如果蔬明显有污垢且你不想让其进入冰箱，确保用干净的纸巾彻底擦干。

Johnston指出，不必试图去除苹果上的蜡质涂层。苹果本身会产生天然蜡质以防止细菌并保持水分，但采收后的田间清洗会去除这层保护膜。为了防止水果腐烂，生产商会在运往商店前添加食品级蜡。"只要生产商遵守FDA的要求，这些涂层就是安全的。"

草莓、莓果和其他软皮水果容易受损，因此不适合用刷子清洗。去除有损伤的部分或直接处理可疑的个体，防止它们影响整个果篮。然后将水果放入滤网中，用冷流水冲洗，理想情况下用厨房喷头。也可以采用与菠菜等叶类蔬菜相同的浸泡冲洗法。

西红柿、成熟桃子和其他嫩皮水果也适用此方法。

对于坚果类根蔬、甜瓜和热带水果如木瓜，用专用刷子在冷流水下刷洗。包括那些可食用果皮的产品（如土豆、胡萝卜），以及那些需要去皮的产品。为什么要清洗即将被扔掉的果皮？因为每次切割时，果皮上的污垢和细菌都会转移到内部。

Johnston建议："清洗完果蔬后，一定要清洁和消毒刷子。" 如果是可放入洗碗机的刷子，非常方便。直接放入洗碗机，下次使用时即可准备就绪。

对于香草束，在使用前放入滤网，用冷流水冲洗。一边冲洗一边用手搓揉，并给予充分晃动。也可以采用上述的浸泡冲洗法。

芫荽和香菜最近被怀疑与环孢子虫疫情有关，Wagner建议关注政府机构的召回通知和指导，确保安全。

葡萄、樱桃等小颗粒水果有许多缝隙，可能让人误以为需要浸泡才能彻底清洗。Wagner指出："很容易认为水中浸泡时间越长，果蔬就越干净，但实际上完全相反。" 只有从水龙头流出的流动水才是清洗这些食物的最安全方式。"

清洗葡萄和樱桃时，应在食用前立即进行，而不是提前。摘除果梗，将水果放入滤网中。如果可能，用厨房喷头喷洗，或在冷流水下冲洗。用洁净的双手轻轻揉搓水果，并在最后冲洗后摇晃滤网。

长期以来，有关蘑菇的建议是用湿纸巾擦拭表面污垢。但像其他含水量和营养价值高的果蔬一样，蘑菇为微生物生长提供了理想环境，这一点在《微生物学前沿》2026年发表的研究中得到证实。

因此，可以遵循蘑菇委员会的建议，用冷流水冲洗蘑菇。务必在使用前进行，而不是提前清洗。喷头很有用，也可以用手指揉搓蘑菇以去除附着的污垢。我已经用这种方法清洗蘑菇多年，没有发现任何质地或水分问题，但用干净的纸巾擦干效果更佳。

FDA和食品安全专家对十字花科蔬菜的指导意见类似：用冷流水冲洗。我喜欢将菜头倒置放在水流下，让水流过所有裂缝，然后给予充分晃动，最后在滤网中冲洗。

如果你有自种的西兰花或花椰菜，科罗拉多州立大学扩展服务建议，可以通过在盐水中浸泡几分钟来鼓励虫子离开（4汤匙盐溶于1加仑水）。确保充分冲洗。

Johnston指出："这些方法没有被证明比冷流水冲洗和刷洗更有效。" 至少在对抗细菌和其他微生物方面。她补充说，果蔬清洗剂和家庭偏方并不是真正的消毒剂。"因此，你真的不需要在这些产品上花钱。"

Wagner表示："小苏打最近有研究支持，其去除表面农药的效果比水或其他溶液更好。" 关键在于，小苏打仅适用于表面农药，渗入果皮的农药即使浸泡小苏打也难以去除。" 这方面的研究正在发展，政府机构和科学家继续强调只使用冷流水。

Have you had a nice big salad lately? If the daily onslaught of news about Cyclospora outbreaks and recalls caused by fresh lettuce has you reaching for the canned corn instead, I get it. I worked for more than a decade at a food safety laboratory, and the list of foods I considered never eating again got pretty long. But I never gave up on fresh fruits and veggies, because often the line between getting sick and feeling great is as simple as cleaning them the right way.

That’s where things tend to go off the rails. When we’re in our own kitchens, we tend to get a little complacent. We clean regularly, we wipe up spills promptly—what’s the big deal if a grape rolls into the sink? Usually, everything’s fine, but germs don’t care about the five-second rule, or how clean your kitchen looks. Even if you’re diligent, you might be doing things completely wrong by following outdated safety advice or faddish trends making the rounds on social media.

Ahead, I talk to Amy Johnston, the statewide food safety educator with the University of Minnesota Extension, and Steve Wagner, an attorney who specializes in foodborne illness litigation, to cut through the bad advice and give you solid, science-backed ways to improve your chances of not getting sick when preparing fresh fruits and vegetables. Read on, and dig in.

Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more food safety, cleaning, humor, travel, tech and fun facts all week long.

Before you start: Here’s what to know

Your first step to clean produce is clean tools: cutting boards, knives, dishes and hands. The FDA recommends washing hands with warm, soapy water for at least 20 seconds before and after cleaning any produce. Next, “always take a moment to clean and sanitize the sink, including the faucet, the drain and any kind of surrounding counter space,” Johnston says. Always use sanitizers that are labeled food safe, she says.

The next hard-and-fast rule is to use cool, running water only. “Warm or hot water can cause certain produce to go through a shock,” Johnston says. “So if there is anything on the outside of that produce, it can get sucked in through the skin or peel into the fleshy part that you’re going to eat.” Wagner says the same goes for soap: “Never use any soaps or detergents, and certainly no bleach, as your produce can absorb the residue.”

Use a produce brush to scrub produce that can handle it (the list is coming up). “Those bristles can really help get into the nooks and crannies that can trap different kinds of contaminants and dirt,” Johnston says.

Finally, it’s important to keep in mind that no cleaning protocol will eliminate all risk. These safe practices are proven to reduce the presence of microorganisms, not get rid of them entirely.

What about the Cyclospora parasite?

“Unfortunately, with Cyclospora, the only way to get rid of it is to cook the produce to at least 158 degrees Fahrenheit,” Johnston says, which is not ideal for produce that’s usually eaten raw. “People think washing it handles the problem, though it’s a bit more detailed, since a rinse can get rid of surface bacteria, but a parasite needs heat to be completely neutralized,” Wagner adds.

“As for E. coli or Salmonella, just running water with friction applied to the surfaces, and keeping it refrigerated below 40 degrees, is usually enough when there’s not an outbreak like this going on,” Wagner says. “During an outbreak, as we currently have, just stay informed of what’s being announced by government agencies, which might, in some cases, be to skip a certain product entirely for the time being.”

That’s great advice right now, especially when it comes to bagged lettuce and other produce implicated in current outbreaks. Normally, food-safety experts do not recommend re-washing bagged produce due to cross-contamination concerns. But the CDC now advises washing all produce, no matter what. Buying whole heads of lettuce, from local farmers if possible, can also bring peace of mind.

Here’s how to clean eight major groups of fruits and vegetables.

Leafy vegetables

For years I filled up my sink and soaked bunches of spinach, lettuce and kale to remove grit. What I didn’t realize is that this could actually introduce more germs than I was removing. “If there were any contaminants on that produce, they could absorb them if you’re letting them soak,” Johnston says. That’s because the delicate leaves are porous (yes, even hearty kale) and can take up contaminants as they sit in the water.

Instead, discard the exterior leaves and rinse the rest under cool running water. If the bunches came from your garden or the farmers market and you’re worried about grit, you can do a “plunge,” Johnston says. Put the leafy greens in a large colander, then dunk them repeatedly into a large bowl or clean sink filled with cool water. Drain and rinse with fresh running water.

Apples and firm veggies like squashes and cucumbers

“Firm produce should be scrubbed under running water with a produce brush or even your clean hands to remove any pathogens,” Wagner says. But don’t do it when you get home from the store; wait until right before you eat or prepare them. This promotes a longer shelf life and reduces the chance of early spoilage (this is true of all produce). If you have to rinse early, like if the produce is visibly dirty and you don’t want that in your fridge, make sure to dry the produce well with a clean paper towel.

What about the waxy coating on apples? Johnston says you do not have to try to remove this. Apples actually produce their own natural wax as protection against bacteria and to retain moisture, but field washing after harvest strips it away. To keep the fruit from spoiling, producers add a food-safe wax before shipping to stores. “As long as producers are following FDA requirements, then those coatings are safe to eat,” Johnston says.

Berries and soft-skinned fruit

Strawberries, raspberries and other fruits with soft skin bruise easily, so skip the scrub brush here. Cut off bruised areas or throw away suspect individual berries so they don’t spoil the whole bunch. Then place berries in a colander and rinse under cool running water, ideally with a kitchen sprayer. (You can also do the dunking method like with spinach and other leafy veggies.)

Tomatoes, ripe peaches and anything with delicate skin also fall into this category.

Root vegetables, melons and produce you peel

For hearty root veggies, melons and tropical fruits like papaya, get out the produce brush and give them a good scrub under cool running water. This goes for things with edible peels, like potatoes and carrots, as well as produce where the peel gets discarded. Why wash a peel you plan to throw out? Because with every slice of the knife, dirt and germs on the outside will get transferred to the inside.

“When you’re done washing produce, clean and sanitize that scrub brush,” Johnston says. “If you have one that’s dishwasher safe, that’s great.” Just throw it in the dishwasher so it’s ready the next time you use it.

Herbs

For bunches of herbs, wait until you are about to use them, then place them in a colander and rinse under cool running water. Give them a good shake and turn them with your hands as you rinse. You can also do the plunge as described above.

Cilantro and parsley were recently suspected in a Cyclospora outbreak, so follow Wagner’s advice and stay alert to recalls and guidance from government agencies to stay safe.

Grapes and cherries

There are lots of nooks and crannies in small, clustered fruits like grapes and cherries, so you might think you need to soak them to get them clean. Nope. “It’s easy to think that more time in water will make produce cleaner, but it’s the total opposite,” Wagner says. “Only moving water running out of the tap is the safest way to clean these foods.”

Clean grapes and cherries right before you plan to eat them, not before. De-stem the fruit and place it in a colander. Spray them with a kitchen sprayer if possible, or hold them under cool running water. Use your clean hands to gently massage the fruits between your fingers, and give the colander a good shake after doing the final rinse.

Mushrooms

For years, the guidance around mushrooms was to just wipe them with a damp paper towel to remove surface dirt. But, like other moisture- and nutrient-dense fruits and vegetables, mushrooms provide an ideal environment for microbial growth, according to a 2026 study published in Frontiers in Microbiology.

So go ahead and follow the Mushroom Council’s advice and rinse mushrooms under cool running water. Do this right before using them, not before. A sprayer works great here, as does rubbing the mushrooms with your fingers to remove clinging dirt. I’ve been rinsing mushrooms for years and haven’t noticed any problems with texture or water retention, but pat them dry with a clean paper towel for best results.

Broccoli and cauliflower

Guidance from the FDA and food safety experts on cruciferous vegetables sounds familiar: Rinse with cool running water. I like to hold the head upside down as the water runs through all the crevices and give it a good shake, then rinse it in a colander.

If you have broccoli or cauliflower fresh from the garden, the Colorado State University Extension says you can encourage bugs to leave the heads by soaking them for a few minutes in salt water (4 tablespoons salt to 1 gallon of water). Make sure to rinse well.

What about using baking soda, vinegar and produce washes?

“None of those have been shown to be more effective than just washing and scrubbing under cool running water,” Johnston says, at least when it comes to bacteria and other microorganisms. She adds that produce washes and home remedies are not sanitizers anyway. “So you really don’t have to spend your money on those other things,” Johnston says.

“Baking soda is backed by recent research showing better removal of pesticides on the surface compared to just water or other solutions,” Wagner says. “The key here is that it’s just ideal for surface pesticides, as anything that has penetrated the skin is harder to remove even with soaking in baking soda.” Research is evolving on this front, and government agencies and scientific experts continue to stress the use of cool running water only.

在美东地区生活，夏季炎热潮湿的天气让人难以忍受。气温升至30℃以上时，外出几分钟就能汗流浃背，即使穿最薄的衣物也像披着羊毛衫。睡眠质量更是无从谈起。

研究表明，极端高温不但令人烦躁易怒，甚至可能引发暴力行为。美东地区医生布莱娜·康纳和拉切尔·马奎斯解释了高温影响情绪的科学原因。

据《自然》期刊子刊《可持续发展通讯》2026年研究，短暂升温会增加暴力事件发生率，包括人际间和自残行为。温度升高后，暴力相关就医人次显著增加，尤其在高温初期两天内。另一研究发现，洛杉矶温度超过21℃时，暴力犯罪率上升。

2023年韩国研究得出相似结论：温度升高增加他杀风险，男性、青少年和受教育程度较低者更易受影响。监狱中缺乏空调和通风系统，温度超过27℃时暴力事件概率增加。

这一现象称为"温度-侵略假说"，高温还影响人际交往的感知。2000年研究发现，人在不适温度下更易感受他人敌意。

人体应对高温需释放压力激素皮质醇和肾上腺素，导致烦躁感加剧。康纳医生解释，人体能量有限，高温使能量消耗在维持体温（36-37℃），减少用于注意力和情绪调节。

马奎斯医生表示，高温触发应激反应，身体通过扩张血管、加速心跳和大量出汗散热。大脑也受影响，注意力下降、反应迟缓、决策困难。

前额叶皮层在高温下效率降低，但情绪中枢仍活跃，导致情绪失控。康纳医生说："小事可能被放大，因为身体已经处于应激状态。高温降低情绪调节能力，易引发激动或易怒反应。"

大量出汗易脱水，导致头痛、疲劳、注意力不集中、易怒和思维迟钝。高温还影响睡眠，而睡眠是情绪稳定的重要因素。马奎斯医生提醒，高温时核心体温难以降低，影响入睡和睡眠质量。

高温导致的烦躁是正常反应，但也是热衰竭的征兆，伴随头痛、恶心、眩晕和冷汗。马奎斯医生警告："从烦躁到混乱或激动可能发展为中暑，需立即就医。"

高温对公众健康威胁严重，尤其老年人、儿童和慢性病患者更易受害。要关注孤独者，提防热中暑等热相关疾病。

应对高温情绪波动的建议：
1. 多喝水。高温加速脱水，即使轻微脱水也引发头痛和易怒。康纳医生建议全天分次饮水，剧烈出汗后补充电解质。
2. 调整活动时间。将户外锻炼改在清晨或傍晚，避免中午高温。可转移至健身房或进行轻度拉伸。
3. 社交活动。与亲友聚会能提升心情。建议在咖啡店或酒吧见面，但避免过量咖啡和酒精。
4. 适当进食。高温抑制食欲，但空腹易导致"饿怒"。康纳医生建议选择冷食、水果、蔬菜、酸奶或沙拉，避免重口味食物增加代谢热。
5. 穿着选择。避免紧身衣、深色和合成纤维。选择轻薄、宽松的浅色棉质或亚麻材质衣物。
6. 屋内降温。保持窗帘关闭，使用风扇，夜间开窗通风，白天关窗保温。冰敷额头、手腕和脚踝，浸泡脚部或冲凉。

高温时保持冷静，关注体温变化，及时采取降温措施，保护身体健康。

There’s a common phrase about summertime weather where I live in the Mid-Atlantic: “It’s not the heat that gets you. It’s the humidity.” Whatever it is, when the temperature climbs into the high 80s and beyond, it’s pretty miserable. Being outdoors for mere minutes can leave you dripping with sweat, and wearing even the thinnest of clothing can feel like you’ve donned a wool sweater. And sleeping soundly? Forget about it.

Even the most calm, cheerful and mild-mannered among us might notice their mood worsens on extremely hot days. And they’re right: The heat can make us feel cranky, irritable or downright angry—and there’s a scientific reason for it.

I talked to Brynna Connor, MD, a family medicine physician and health-care ambassador at Northwest Pharmacy, and Rachel Marquez, MD, a family medicine doctor and regional medical director of external affairs at Kaiser Permanente Mid-Atlantic, to find out why the heat affects our mood. I also dug into the latest research about this sweltering phenomenon, so keep reading to learn what you can do to stay cool out there.

Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more science, cleaning, humor, travel, tech and fun facts all week long.

How bad can things get when it’s ridiculously hot out?

Pretty bad, which is especially concerning now, given that we’re experiencing more heat stress days more often—up to 50 more days per year in some places, according to the latest research. Nights are getting hotter and staying hotter too.

A 2026 study published in the Nature Portfolio journal Communications Sustainability found a link between even short-term spikes in temperature and greater incidence of violence, both interpersonal and self-inflicted. Researchers found that as the temperature rose, the number of violence-related hospital visits increased, particularly in the first two days of high heat. Another study discovered that when temperatures exceeded a mild 70 degrees, there were more violent crimes in Los Angeles.

In 2023, researchers in South Korea came to the same conclusion: The risk of deaths by assault increased as temperatures rose, especially among males, teenagers and those with less education. In prisons, which often lack adequate air-conditioning and ventilation, the probability of violence rose when temperatures climbed above 80 degrees.

This phenomenon is called the temperature-aggression or heat-aggression hypothesis, and it can even affect our interpretations of conversations and people’s tone. And researchers have been keying in on this for decades: A 2000 study found that when we’re uncomfortably hot, we perceive other people and other interactions as being more hostile.

What happens to your body in extreme heat?

Extreme heat triggers the body’s stress response as it fights to keep cool. Part of that response is the release of the stress hormones cortisol and adrenaline, which “increase the feeling of restlessness and being on edge,” says Dr. Marquez.

The body has a limited amount of energy available to it at any given time, explains Dr. Connor. On extremely hot days, the body expends a lot of that energy keeping our core body temperature at normal levels (between 97 and 99 degrees). “This leaves less energy available for things like concentration and emotional regulation,” she says.

In order to keep the body cool, Dr. Connor says, the “blood vessels in the skin enlarge to release heat, your heart pumps more rapidly to bring the blood to the skin, and you sweat more to cool yourself through evaporation.”

Hot days can also stress out our brains, which must also stay within an optimal temperature range to function properly. “When body temperature rises, your attention span decreases, reaction time slows and decision-making becomes more difficult,” Dr. Connor says.

Why does this make us so grumpy—or even outright angry?

The body perceives extreme heat as more than just discomfort. “The reason we get more irritable and grumpy when the weather is really hot is that our bodies are experiencing real physiological stress, which changes how both the brain and body function,” Dr. Connor says. The brain’s prefrontal cortex, which is responsible for impulse control, judgment and emotional regulation, doesn’t work as efficiently and effectively in extreme heat. But the emotional centers of our brains do stay active. This combination can translate to anger and impulsivity.

“Little triggers can feel larger or more significant, since the body is already under stress,” Dr. Connor says. “Heat can lower the threshold for aggressive or irritable responses as it becomes more difficult for the brain to regulate emotions.”

Because we’re sweating more to cool down, it’s easier to become dehydrated. “Sweating causes you to lose both water and electrolytes, such as sodium and potassium,” Dr. Connor says. “Even mild dehydration can result in symptoms like headache, fatigue, difficulty concentrating, irritability and slower cognitive processing.”

Heat also makes sleeping practically impossible—and we all know we’re not our best selves after a night of bad sleep. “Sleep is one of the best tools we have for keeping our emotions balanced,” Dr. Marquez says. Our core body temperature has to drop to fall and stay asleep, and that is really tricky in sweltering heat.

Does grumpiness or anger in extreme heat signal a more serious health issue?

Irritability is a normal response to the heat, Dr. Marquez says, but it’s also one of the recognized symptoms of heat exhaustion, along with headache, nausea, dizziness and cold, clammy skin.

“Watch for the change from irritable to confused or agitated, since that can mean that heat exhaustion could be progressing toward heatstroke, which is a medical emergency,” Dr. Marquez says. “If you or someone with you is experiencing confusion, a seizure, hot, dry skin or loss of consciousness, call 911 right away. Grumpy is normal. Confused is not.”

High temperatures can pose serious—and potentially deadly—health risks. “Extreme heat is a community-wide health concern,” Dr. Marquez says. “Check in on the people around you, especially those who live alone. Older adults, young children and people managing chronic health conditions can be particularly vulnerable to heat-related illness.”

How can we keep our cool in the heat?

If the heat is starting to make your blood boil, here are some tips for managing your mood and cooling off.

Stay hydrated

If you’re feeling grumpy, foggy or generally out of sorts, drink a glass of water (or two). More heat means more sweating, which means faster dehydration. Even slight dehydration can cause headaches and irritability.

“Drink water throughout the day instead of waiting until you’re thirsty,” Dr. Connor says. “If you’ve been sweating heavily for several hours, you may also need drinks with electrolytes to replace what’s been lost.”

Shift your outdoor routines

Physical activity and spending time outdoors are normally two of the best ways to relieve stress and boost your mood, but doing those things when it’s really hot isn’t the best idea. Tweak your routine a bit.

“If your routine typically includes outdoor exercise, yard work or other time outside, consider moving those activities indoors, rescheduling them for cooler parts of the day or taking more frequent breaks from the heat,” Dr. Marquez says.

Try running on the treadmill at the gym instead of outside. Move your usual post-lunch walk to early morning or evening to avoid the midday sun. Even light stretching or yoga can help you feel better.

Socialize with others

When it’s really hot, we might want to hunker down inside with the AC. But getting out and spending time with friends or family can improve your mood. Catch up with a friend over an iced coffee or chilled cocktail (though don’t overdo it, as coffee and alcohol can increase dehydration). Take it from kids: Water can cheer most anyone up, so gather some people to hang out at a local pool, lake or stream.

Make sure you’re eating enough

We often don’t feel like eating much when it’s extremely hot, but a grumbling stomach can quickly turn into “hanger.” Plus, the body is working overtime to regulate our body temperatures and needs those calories for fuel.

Dr. Connor recommends keeping meals light. “Eating cold foods, fruits, vegetables, yogurt or salads can help you feel more comfortable on hot days,” she says. “Large or heavy meals can increase heat production due to digestion.”

Dress smart

Some colors and fabrics can trap heat and moisture, making us feel even hotter and more uncomfortable. Skip heavy denim, dark colors, form-fitting outfits and synthetic fabrics. Even your jewelry might need an overhaul. Gold and silver jewelry are conductors and will trap heat close to the body.

“Wear lightweight, loose-fitting fabrics, ideally in light colors, in breathable materials such as cotton, linen or other moisture-wicking fabrics,” Dr. Connor says.

How can you lower your body temperature quickly if there’s no AC in sight?

Even if you live or work somewhere without air-conditioning, there are still steps you can take to cool down. Here’s what the experts suggest:

  • Keep window blinds, shades or curtains closed during the hottest hours of the day, typically between 3 and 6 p.m. Open them back up at night, when the temperature cools down.
  • Apply a cool, damp towel or splash cold water on parts of the body where large blood vessels are close to the skin: neck, wrists, forearms and behind the knees. Immersing your hands in cold water for a few minutes will also bring your temperature down.
  • Take a cool shower, drench your shirt in water or mist yourself with a cooling spray or cold water.
  • Try to find some AC. If you can get access to any air-conditioning, like a single window unit in a bedroom or at a public place like a library, sit in that space long enough for your core temperature to come down, not just your skin, Dr. Connor says. “Typically this occurs within 30 to 60 minutes, but in instances of heat stress or heat exhaustion, it could take up to 24 to 48 hours, plus fluid replenishment,” she says.

Sources:
